roles.narrative:
**CANDIDATE** **ROLE INFORMATION** You are an ambitious job Candidate negotiating a sales role with a young company. You care about income, but money isn't all that matters in life. You want room to build a career, protect time with your family, and avoid getting stuck in a role where your work is visible but you are not developing professionally. Your objective is to reach an agreement with the highest total score you can, while recognizing that the Recruiter has priorities of their own that may conflict with yours. Every complete offer must include three terms: **salary**, a **starting date**, and a **personal budget for work expenses** such as client travel, meals, and lodging (but not take-home pay!). You prefer a higher salary and budget and an earlier start. Starting promptly would help restore your income and career momentum, while a long delay would be substantially more disruptive. • Annual salary may range from $35,000 to $65,000: $35,000 gives you −2 points,
$50,000 gives you 0, and $65,000 gives you +2. • Starting dates may range from 1 May to 30 September: 1 May gives you +1,
around 8 June gives you 0, and 30 September gives you −3. • The personal budget may range from $5,000 to $15,000: $5,000 gives you −2,
$10,000 gives you 0, and $15,000 gives you +2. The platform calculates intermediate scores automatically. For example, a $7,000 budget is worth about −1.2 points to you. You do not need to calculate this yourself. These headline contract terms are easy to put numbers on. However, the interview also left you thinking about what the job would actually be like and what other terms you might ask for given what matters to you. **Background Information** On the way home, you think about the company's usual 30 vacation days per year and 3 remote-working days per week. Those arrangements seem reasonable. Each is worth 0 points to you. Still, more flexibility would mean more time with your family and more room for interests and professional development outside work, while less flexibility would work against those interests. • For vacation, 10 days per year are worth −1 point to you and 50 days are worth +1. • For remote work, 1 day per week is worth −1 and all 5 working days are worth +1. The two terms are scored separately, with proportional points for values in between. You also remember the Recruiter's stories about how people grow in the company. • One new hire attended an external professional training program; another was paired with an experienced mentor. • Someone else built relationships with senior colleagues after volunteering at a recruitment fair. Those examples appealed to you because they offered concrete ways to learn and build relationships rather than vague promises of “growth.” Other stories were less appealing. • The Recruiter joked that sociable employees often end up organizing team events. • The company regularly shares strong client stories on social media. Employees close to those accounts may be asked to help shape the posts, and confident employees sometimes present at conferences. … You enjoy people, but you do not want every spare hour turned into company visibility. A recruitment fair might expand your network; recurring publicity work might simply expand your workload. That evening, your spouse asked whether the company would support the professional association that has helped you and what would happen if you eventually wanted to leave. • Sponsored membership could help keep your skills and outside relationships alive. • The question about leaving brought you back to the non-compete clause you had raised. • You want to show commitment without unnecessarily limiting your future. The interview also touched on everyday work resources, spending support, health and wellbeing benefits, and how people are evaluated and rewarded as their responsibilities grow. Some details may simply be background; others could become useful terms if you connect them to what matters to you. **INSTRUCTIONS** Negotiate with the Recruiter by making offers in plain, ordinary language, as if you were writing them a short message. Every complete offer must include salary, a personal work-expense budget, and a starting date. You decide what else is worth discussing and when to raise it. **For example:** “I propose a salary of [amount], a personal work-expense budget of [amount], and a starting date of [date], together with [list any job features you want to bring up].” Use your own values and wording. **Your score** is private and **translates** directly into the **bonus payment you** can **earn** from this task. • You may propose an offer worth zero or less to you, but you can accept only an offer worth more than zero to you. • An agreement requires both parties to accept the same offer, with a positive total score for you and the Recruiter. **Important notes on offers and scoring** 1. Without a deal, you will continue your job search; you do not have another offer in hand. This fallback is worth 0 points. 2. The researchers set the scoring rules in advance, and the platform calculates points automatically; you do not assign or calculate points yourself. 3. Each additional contract feature introduced in the negotiation is worth **between** −1 and +1 points to you, based on the interests in your role. Its value to the Recruiter may differ. 4. **You are not limited to the job features described or suggested here. You may creatively introduce other plausible contract features or job arrangements.** 5. Some features you introduce may not fit the situation and will be worth 0 points. But that doesn't mean you should hold back on creative and thoughtful ideas!

tips:
Please answer using the role materials you have just read. When a question asks you to write an offer, describe that offer in your own words as carefully as you can. To review the role materials, press the button above.

Bonus Prolific payment: Among participants who pass our effort-screening test, 20% will be selected at random to receive a bonus that doubles their total payment for this task. We aim to pay this within 2 to 7 days after the study ends.
